message.content: I heard that near Egyptian Naucratis lived one of the ancient gods of that place, to whom was consecrated the bird called the ibis. The name of this deity — Theut[172]. He first invented number, arithmetic, geometry and astronomy, the game of draughts and dice, and invented [107]also letters. King of all Egypt at that time was D. Famus[173], who sat in a large city of the upper part of the country. This city the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and the god — Ammon. Once Theut, having come to Famus, announced to him his arts and said that it was necessary to communicate them to all the Egyptians; but the latter asked him: what use can each of them provide? When Theut began to explain this, the king, depending on whether the explanation appeared to him good or bad, censured some things and praised others. In general, he said much to Theut E. about each art, in the one direction and the other: to tell about this would take long. Finally the matter came to letters, and Theut said: Sovereign! this science will make the Egyptians wiser and more mindful; I invented it as a means for memory and wisdom. But the king answered: Much-learned Theut! one is able to give birth to arts, and another to judge how much harm or profit they will bring to the people who will use them. Here you, father of letters, from 275. parental love, have ascribed to them the opposite of what they can do. For this, weakening carefulness about remembering, will produce in the souls of the pupils forgetfulness[174]; because, relying on external writing, depicted by foreign signs, they will not recall impressions internally — themselves in [108]themselves. So you have invented a means not for remembering, but for reminding. And wisdom the pupils will acquire[175] from you not true, but seeming; because, having listened to much and studying nothing, they will represent themselves as knowers of much and, as supposed sages, instead of true ones, B. will remain for the most part ignorant and people in society unbearable.

I need to translate this literally into English while preserving the footnote and Stephanus page markers as they appear in the original. Starting with the passage about the Egyptian god near Naucratis associated with the ibis bird.

The deity's name is Theut, who invented numbers, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, games like draughts and dice, and letters. At that time King Famus ruled Egypt from a great city the Greeks call Thebes, associated with the god Ammon. Theut came to Famus to present his inventions and argued they should be shared with all Egyptians, but Famus questioned what benefit each one would actually provide.

When Theut explained each art, the king weighed its merits and flaws, praising some and criticizing others — a lengthy exchange I won't fully detail. Eventually they reached the subject of letters, and Theut claimed this invention would make Egyptians wiser and improve their memory, calling it a remedy for both. But the king's response is where the thought cuts off.

This means the invention is for reminding, not remembering. And the wisdom students gain would be false — having heard much without truly studying, they'll seem knowledgeable while actually remaining ignorant and insufferable in company.
